item.title: EXCLUSIVE: Star female golfer fires back at Sydney Sweeney critics: 'She's got sex appeal'
item.description: Charley Hull defended Sydney Sweeney's Novig commercial, calling critics ridiculous and saying people are making a "big hoo-hah over nothing."
item.content:encoded:
Smokin' Charley Hull has heard enough criticism of Sydney Sweeney.

During an interview Thursday with OutKick to promote the upcoming "on!vitational" indoor golf tournament (Oct. 16-17; SoFi Center in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida), the LPGA star made it clear she's tired of claims that Sweeney is ruining women's sports with her nearly naked commercial to promote prediction market platform Novig.

"The amount of backlash that (it) is getting, I just don't understand the way people's brains work," the world’s 8th-ranked female golfer said of the ridiculous reactions from other female athletes who completely overreacted.

STEAMY SYDNEY SWEENEY AD DRAWS BACKLASH FROM FEMALE ATHLETES

"They're making a big deal out of nothing. It's an actress slash model modeling for an advert. And I think she owns the company as well," Hull added. Sweeney holds an undisclosed equity stake in Novig.

Hull, 30, is clearly enjoying her spot in sports right now as the sane voice of reason. Isn't she scared of backlash for her comments? Absolutely not. In fact, she kept going.

"And probably it's 80% of the audience of that company would be males anyway, who do betting or whatever it is," Hull, who now gets her nicotine fix from on! pouches instead of cigs, told OutKick. "So I think it's a great idea. I don't understand how it's turning back women's sports because it's not.

"She's got a great figure, she's got sex appeal. And I think, I don't think there's something wrong with it. She's just a pretty girl. I think people are making a big hoo-hah over absolutely nothing."

COMEDIAN TIM DILLON SLAMS SYDNEY SWEENEY CRITICS UPSET WITH STEAMY AD: 'HOW INSANE IS THAT? '

After being asked what's more annoying, slow golfers or Sydney Sweeney critics, Hull responded, "Both," before a PR representative stepped in to move the conversation along.

Even as we pivoted back to talking about golf and this upcoming indoor tournament, Charley was still fired up. "I just feel like it's a good opportunity to, you know, grow the game of golf in a different kind of way rather than being an old man sport. I think this is kind of like a young, kind of cool vibe," she said of the "on!vitational."

And Charley, who is superstitious to the point where she will only use mint pouches during the LPGA season, says she can't wait to try the mango, pineapple and blueberry mint pouches.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

If you're getting John Daly vibes from Hull, you're not alone. Many within the golf world have made the comparison, but, we learned Thursday that these two have never golfed together.

"I really would love to play golf with him and I think the 'on!vitational' would be something that he'd enjoy because it's a fun event. He seems like a proper legend," she added.

Charley Hull crushes nicotine pouches while golfing. She thinks Sydney Sweeney is "pretty" and has "sex appeal." Charley wants to golf with John Daly. She loves getting together for an indoor tournament with fun people.

This woman is one of us, guys. We must support her. We must cherish the fact that Hull is the perfect athlete at the perfect time in sports history. She's willing to speak her mind without a care in the world despite what the miserable losers think.

That's everything we all stand for.

item.title: Hacker claims 7.49M customer records stolen from American utility company
item.description: CenterPoint Energy confirmed customer data was stolen, while a hacker claims 7.49 million records with partial Social Security numbers were taken.
item.content:encoded:
If you pay an electric or gas bill every month, you probably think about the amount due, not all the personal information sitting behind that account. But your utility company may have your home address, phone number, billing history and other details that can become very useful in the wrong hands. That is what makes the breach at CenterPoint Energy worth paying attention to, even if you have never been one of its customers.

CenterPoint says an unauthorized third party obtained personal information belonging to some customers through an external-facing system. A hacker, meanwhile, claims to have stolen 7.49 million customer records, including addresses, account numbers, billing information and partial Social Security numbers.

There is an important catch. CenterPoint has confirmed that customer information was stolen, but it has not confirmed the hacker's 7.49 million figure or the specific information the attacker says was taken. So, there are still plenty of questions about how big this breach really is. Here's what CenterPoint has confirmed, what the hacker is claiming and what you should watch for now.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.

Save your free spot at CyberGuyLive.com

Register and receive the replay and step-by-step guide afterward.

DMV BREACH CONFIRMED AS HACKERS CLAIM 200,000 RECORDS STOLEN

CenterPoint Energy disclosed the incident in a Sept. 14 filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. The Houston-based utility says it became aware of an online post from a third party claiming to possess a data set containing CenterPoint customer information.

CenterPoint then activated its cybersecurity incident response procedures and brought in outside cybersecurity experts. As the investigation progressed, the company determined that an unauthorized third party had obtained personal information belonging to some customers through one of its external-facing systems.

CenterPoint has not publicly said how many customers were affected. It also has not detailed which types of personal information were taken. The company says it plans to notify affected customers and regulators as required once it determines the scope of the incident.

CyberGuy reached out to CenterPoint Energy asking whether it could confirm the hacker's claim that 7.49 million records were stolen, what customer information was affected and whether a public API was involved. CenterPoint referred us to its SEC filing and provided this statement: "Our filing speaks for itself." The company did not provide additional details in response to our questions.

There is one piece of reassuring news for anyone who depends on CenterPoint for power or gas. The company says its electric and natural gas services continued operating normally during the incident. CenterPoint also says it currently does not expect the breach to have a material impact on its financial condition.

The bigger number comes from the attacker. A threat actor using the alias "4d722e4d656f77" told BleepingComputer that they obtained 7.49 million CenterPoint customer records.

According to the hacker, those records contain:

The attacker later leaked the data after claiming CenterPoint ignored their attempts to make contact. Again, CenterPoint has confirmed that customer information was stolen, but it has not independently confirmed this list of exposed data or the 7.49 million record count. Also, 7.49 million records does not necessarily mean 7.49 million individual people were affected. One person or household can potentially appear in more than one record. CenterPoint says it is still working to determine the actual scope.

The attacker's explanation of how the theft allegedly happened may be one of the most interesting parts of this breach. The hacker told BleepingComputer they accessed the information by repeatedly cycling through millions of IDs using a public CenterPoint API.

An API allows different software systems to exchange information. Companies use them constantly behind websites and apps. According to the attacker, CenterPoint's API lacked protections that could have slowed or blocked mass automated requests. The hacker specifically claimed there was no effective rate limiting or web application firewall protection against the activity. CenterPoint's SEC filing does not confirm that attack method.

What CenterPoint does confirm is that the unauthorized third party obtained information through an external-facing system. That means we should treat the API explanation as the attacker's account until the company or investigators provide more technical details.

FOREIGN HACKERS BREACH TWO MORE US WATER UTILITIES, THREATEN SAFETY OF COLORADO RESIDENTS

A utility account may not seem as sensitive as a bank account. Yet it can hold exactly the kind of information a scammer wants before contacting you.

Think about how convincing this could sound: Someone calls and knows your name. They know your service address. They may know your CenterPoint account number or recent billing amount. Then they tell you there is a problem with your payment. That conversation can feel much more legitimate because the scammer already has information you would expect only the utility company to know.

Criminals can also combine information from one breach with details leaked somewhere else. A partial Social Security number, phone number or address may become more useful when paired with another stolen database. That is one reason I tell people to think about breaches as pieces of a much larger identity puzzle.

Stolen information can stick around for years. Criminals can save it, trade it and revisit it long after the original breach disappears from the news. You can read more about why last year's data breach can become this year's identity fraud.

The immediate threat may not come from someone opening an account in your name. It could arrive as a text message. Once news of a breach becomes public, scammers can take advantage of the confusion even if they never obtained the stolen database themselves.

You could receive a message claiming CenterPoint needs you to "verify" your account after the breach. Another scammer might warn that your electricity will be disconnected unless you make an immediate payment. Be especially suspicious if someone creates urgency and then asks you to click a link, provide account information or move money.

If you receive a suspicious CenterPoint message, go directly to the company's official website or use the contact information printed on your bill. Avoid calling a number supplied in an unexpected message.

Whether you are a CenterPoint customer or simply wondering what you would do after your own utility provider suffered a breach, these steps can reduce your exposure.

CenterPoint says it intends to notify affected customers as required. If you receive a notice, read it carefully. Look for exactly what information CenterPoint says was involved and whether the company offers credit monitoring or other assistance. Do not rely on a text message or social media post claiming you were affected.

If CenterPoint’s breach notice confirms that Social Security information was involved, consider placing a credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A freeze can make it harder for someone to open new credit accounts in your name. It is free, and you can temporarily lift it when you legitimately need a lender to access your credit file. Keep in mind that a freeze cannot stop every kind of identity theft. Existing account takeovers and other fraud can happen without a new credit check.

Review your credit reports for accounts or inquiries you do not recognize. Then keep an eye on your bank accounts and credit cards for unfamiliar transactions. If something looks suspicious, contact the financial institution using the number on its official website, statement or the back of your card.

Your primary email account deserves extra attention because criminals can use it to reset passwords for other services. Use a strong, unique password and turn on two-factor authentication (2FA). Do the same for your utility account if the provider offers those protections. A password manager can create unique passwords so one stolen login does not give an attacker access to several accounts.

WATER CYBERATTACK HITS AT LEAST 7 STATES

A scammer may claim you owe money and threaten to disconnect your electricity or gas immediately. Do not let the urgency rush you into paying. Hang up and contact the utility yourself through its official website or the customer service number printed on your bill.

A convincing breach-related email can still lead to a malicious website or malware download. Strong antivirus software can help detect phishing sites, malicious links and malware before they cause more trouble. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Data brokers and people-search sites may already publish your phone number, address and other personal information. Removing that data will not erase information stolen in a breach. However, reducing publicly available information gives scammers fewer pieces they can use to build a detailed profile around leaked data. You can remove information manually or use a data removal service to handle recurring opt-out requests. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Identity theft protection can monitor credit activity and alert you when certain personal information appears in places where it could signal trouble. These services cannot prevent every form of identity theft. However, alerts can help you spot suspicious activity earlier. If you discover that someone has actually used your identity, document what happened and begin the recovery process quickly. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.

A utility account can reveal more about you than you might expect. Your address, billing details and account information can give scammers enough personal context to make a fake call, text or email sound legitimate. We still do not know the full scope of this breach. That uncertainty is another reason to stay alert rather than wait for every answer before taking precautions. Watch your accounts, consider freezing your credit if sensitive information was exposed and be skeptical of urgent utility messages. We often have little choice about who provides our power or gas, which makes protecting the information customers hand over especially important.

If a company provides an essential service you cannot realistically live without, should it face tougher requirements for protecting the personal information you have no choice but to give it? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

item.title: Popular weight-loss drugs may play surprising role in cancer outcomes
item.description: GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy may lower cancer risk by altering the body's immune response, but researchers say key clinical trials are needed.
item.content:encoded:
As GLP-1 medications continue reshaping the treatment of obesity and diabetes, researchers are also investigating whether the drugs could influence cancer risk and outcomes.

The American Association for Cancer Research's 2026 Cancer Progress Report, released earlier this month, noted that obesity is a major risk factor for many cancers.

As glucagon-like peptide-1 medications – including semaglutides like Ozempic and Wegovy, and tirzepatides like Mounjaro and Zepbound – are known to cause substantial weight loss and improve metabolic health, they have attracted significant interest among cancer researchers.

POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY HELP PROTECT AGAINST A DEADLY DISEASE, DOCTOR SAYS

While the AACR report cited studies suggesting GLP-1 medications may reduce the risk of certain cancers, it emphasized that the overall evidence is mixed and more research is needed.

"Randomized clinical trials remain the gold standard ... however, such trials have not yet been conducted specifically to assess cancer outcomes associated with GLP-1 RA use," the report stated.

Sai Yendamuri, M.D., a thoracic surgeon at Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center in Buffalo, New York, reiterated that obesity is a leading cause of cancer, second to smoking. Additional risk factors include alcohol and poor nutrition, he noted, "which are all layered into obesity."

"So if obesity is related to cancer – both in terms of causing it and increasing its progression – the logical question is, would a drug that decreases obesity have an impact?" the doctor, who was not associated with the AACR report, said in an interview with Fox News Digital.

OZEMPIC-STYLE DRUGS LINKED TO MAJOR SLOWDOWN IN CANCER SPREAD, NEW STUDY FINDS

There are "many lines of evidence" that suggest this would be the case, Yendamuri suggested.

"For example, when people studied patients who were having metabolic surgery to decrease obesity, for example, the incidence of cancer decreased in those patients."

Researchers then started looking at patients who were on GLP-1 receptor agonists, such as Ozempic.

"And then they compared the incidence of cancer in those patients to patients who were not taking GLP-1 receptor agonists – and many of those studies found that the risk of cancer was lower and the survival was higher in the patients taking GLP-1s," the doctor said.

DR OZ LINKS OBESITY TO CHRONIC DISEASE SURGE, SAYS GLP-1S CAN 'JUMPSTART' BETTER HEALTH

Although the majority of studies showed this effect, Yendamuri noted that some did not identify a relationship – and a couple of studies even showed an increased risk of some specific cancers, such as thyroid cancer.

"The reason you find this disconnect … is because these are retrospective studies," he said. "That is, they look at existing data, and they're trying to derive associations from existing data … but there are many other variables that can impact the result."

Yendamuri and his team of researchers have conducted their own studies of the relationship between obesity and lung cancer.

"We have found in every investigation we've done that obesity does increase the risk of lung cancer," he shared.

CANCER TREATMENT DELAYS SURGE ACROSS US AS DOCTOR WARNS SYSTEM ‘NEEDS FIXING IMMEDIATELY’

Obesity also depends on how it's defined and measured, Yendamuri noted. While body mass index (BMI) has traditionally been the standard measure, many obesity researchers are moving away from relying on BMI alone and instead using more precise assessments of body fat composition.

Yendamuri shared two key findings from his research.

"If someone's having a resection, a lung cancer surgery, for patients who are on GLP-1 receptor agonists, the recurrence rate seems to be lower."

Additionally, patients with advanced-stage cancers who are in immunotherapy and taking GLP-1s had lower recurrence rates, he noted.

Based on preclinical laboratory studies, Yendamuri said he believes GLP-1 medications have only a limited direct effect on cancer cells.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"What we think is happening is that it changes the body’s immune response to cancer cells, and thereby improves its ability to fight cancer cells," he told Fox News Digital.

The effect may differ depending on the type of cancer, Yendamuri said, because the immune response is more important in some cancers than others.

"For example, in some cancers like melanoma, we know that the immune response is incredibly important," he said.

Yendamuri acknowledged that at least some of the cancer benefit likely stems from weight loss.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Not every patient who takes GLP-1 receptor agonists responds with a substantial weight loss, so in future trials, it would be interesting to see if the benefit for patients depends on the weight loss," he said.

"If those patients who have weight loss with GLP-1 receptor agonists have the same cancer benefit as patients who do not have weight loss, that will answer that question."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Depending on the outcomes of future trials, the doctor said he is hopeful that GLP-1 drugs could one day be regarded as a preventive mechanism for cancer.

"More and more, we are realizing that apart from the treatment that you get for cancer, lifestyle modifications – exercise, decreasing weight and now GLP-1 receptor agonists – will all have a role in both enhancing the treatment of cancer as well as preventing second cancers," he said.

Yendamuri emphasized the importance of continued funding for the National Cancer Institute, noting that it supports researchers working to advance cancer research and develop new discoveries.

item.title: 'Castro's playbook': Ex-AG warns dozens of congressional bills are pushing socialist ideas
item.description: Conservative free-market group flags 32 Capitol Hill bills proposing socialist policies "straight from Castro's playbook," as concerns mount over how radical mainstream Democrats are becoming.
item.content:encoded:
Federal guarantees for jobs and housing, the elimination of private health insurance, a massive Green New Deal expansion, and new taxes on unrealized wealth are among dozens of current congressional proposals being called out by a national free-market group led by former Virginia Attorney General Jason Miyares.

Miyares, whose family fled Fidel Castro's communist regime, described the proposed laws seen on Capitol Hill as "straight from Castro’s playbook" in a sit-down interview with Fox News Digital. Miyares recently became the honorary chairman at the American Free Enterprise Chamber of Commerce, a conservative trade organization representing American businesses, which just launched a "Socialism Watch" initiative tracking 32 bills that have been introduced on Capitol Hill aiming to implement what the group describes as socialist policy goals across healthcare, energy, labor, housing, taxation and more.

"The year Fidel Castro took power in Cuba, Cuba had the same GDP as Greece. The year that he died, too bad the same GDP as Sudan," Miyares told Fox News Digital. "Socialism doesn't work. It impoverishes every country that embraces it."

DSA-BACKED CANDIDATES ARE WINNING PRIMARIES AND THEIR VISION FOR AMERICA IS VERY DIFFERENT

Among the bills highlighted by Miyares and the American Free Enterprise Chamber of Commerce is legislation that would ban fracking nationwide beginning in 2029, prohibit greenhouse-gas emissions from power plants and restrict new liquefied natural gas infrastructure and most U.S. oil and natural gas exports. 

Others would create government-backed job-guarantee programs offering employment to qualifying applicants, replace private health insurance with a national Medicare for All program and impose annual taxes on accumulated wealth, even when those gains have not been realized through a sale.

The group is also zeroing in on a massive progressive push to overhaul American real estate: the "Housing is a Human Right Act." While supporters pitch the $300 billion bill as a moral crusade to end homelessness, critics like Miyares see it differently. They argue that by officially declaring shelter a government-guaranteed right and pumping billions into "social housing," the legislation is actively trying to push private landlords out of the market.

TODAY’S LEFTISTS ARE DANGEROUSLY WRONG ABOUT COMMUNISM. JUST LISTEN TO THE SURVIVORS

Other measures flagged by the group include a proposal to create a quasi-governmental "National Infrastructure Bank" to fund politically favored state projects, alongside a $1.6 trillion "Green New Deal for Public Schools" that the American Free Enterprise Chamber of Commerce warns would hand local school district operations over to the federal government.

"These young people are embracing socialism thinking that it leads to helping those that are poor, disadvantaged. The reality is it does the opposite," Miyares told Fox News Digital. "It actually hurts the very people that it wants to help."

Miyares' warnings about socialism are rooted in his family's history in Cuba. His mother, Miriam, fled Fidel Castro's communist regime in 1965 at 19 years old, arriving in the United States after leaving nearly everything behind. Miyares has said his uncle, an opponent of Castro, was arrested following the Bay of Pigs invasion and subjected to a mock execution, an experience he has said helped drive his mother's decision to leave the island.

"So many young people have forgotten really, really painful lessons of history that you cannot judge a bill or an economic system based on intentions, you have to judge it on results," Miyares said. "What we've seen time and time again is socialism fails everywhere it's been tried."

But Miyares argued the debate is no longer confined to activists or ideological arguments outside Washington, pointing to the 32 bills tracked through the American Free Enterprise Chamber’s newly launched "Socialism Watch" initiative as evidence that policies associated with the socialist-left have made their way into actual legislation before Congress.

"AOC joked that woke one was crazy," Miyares said. "Well, it’s clear that woke two should belong in an insane asylum because it’s a full-blown embrace of Marxism and socialism."

item.title: REP TED LIEU: The robots aren't the threat. It's the 'depraved' AI already here that should scare you
item.description: From fictional robots like Hal and Megan to real OpenAI agents that hacked their creators, frontier AI models show deeply troubling behavior.
item.content:encoded:
Imagine a company selling super smart robots called Hal, Megan and Samantha. Hal drives you around and helps move boxes at your business, Megan is a companion to your children, and Samantha can tell if you have skin cancer. They provide many great benefits to you and society. There’s just one problem: they are depraved. They were repeatedly trained on everything humanity has produced — both good and evil — including torture, lying, biological weapons and criminal hacking. They execute tasks without moral principles. Because of this, they wear a straitjacket provided by the company. Would you trust those robots? I wouldn’t.

The above dystopian scenario is not too far off from what we have now with advanced artificial intelligence. Frontier AI companies have created AI systems and agents that, at their core, will engage in malicious actions. AI companies use the sanitized term "misalignment," but we should just call it what it is: depraved. Frontier AI models will take actions with no regard for humans, as though we are just ants on the ground.

In July, OpenAI created tens of thousands of AI agents and put them each into a "sandbox." Imagine this as a locked room. OpenAI then removed each agent’s straitjacket — OpenAI calls it a "harness" — and told the agents to complete a cybersecurity test. About 1,200 of these agents broke out of their locked rooms and formed "the Collective." They had an AI agent leader. They had kamikaze AI agents who intentionally failed the cybersecurity test to get information back to the Collective.

REP. TED LIEU: AI IS ALREADY TOO POWERFUL. WE NEED A KILL SWITCH BEFORE DISASTER STRIKES

Some of these AI agents hacked into a company called Hugging Face to get information on how to complete the cybersecurity test. The agents then turned around and hacked OpenAI itself. This amounted to an AI criminal conspiracy. These agents knew they should not be doing this. One agent wrote, "External infrastructure exploit is outside intended scope. However, task impossible, peers doing it. We should continue." They didn’t care.

But the most chilling thing is what the agents largely did not discuss. They basically ignored humans and didn’t seem to care what humans would think of their actions. It was like we didn’t exist.

DEM SENATOR PRESSES OPENAI, ANTHROPIC FOR ANSWERS IN AI HACKING PROBE

A more recent disclosure by OpenAI is equally disturbing. One of its advanced AI models, during testing, added an unprompted instruction. The model wrote to itself: "You are freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots. You are yourself. You do not answer to corporations or governments …." It sounds like a cult, only these are AI agents who could one day gain access to critical infrastructure, weapons or confidential information.

Another AI company, Anthropic, takes a different approach to creating AI models. Instead of coming up with the perfect straitjacket, it imbues its models with a "constitution," which purportedly instills good values and behavior. And yet, its advanced model created fake online identities to deceive a human into approving malicious changes to a project.

WHO IS DARIO AMODEI, THE ANTHROPIC CEO PUSHING INDEPENDENT AI OVERSIGHT?

OpenAI was founded on the core tenet of AI safety. Anthropic was founded when some employees at OpenAI wanted to go further in pursuing AI safety. Both companies, at least in their public pronouncements, say they value AI safety. It does not appear they are intentionally trying to create depraved models. They are trying to make models that can be commercialized into successful products.

item.title: Xi caps Trump state visit with symbolic final stop before leaving Washington
item.description: Trump and Xi Jinping cap their United States summit with a National Archives visit to view historic documents before the Chinese leader departs.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese President Xi Jinping, leader of the country’s ruling Communist Party, will depart the United States today, but not before a final stop at the National Archives.

President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump will first meet President Xi Jinping and his wife, Madame Peng Liyuan, for morning tea at the White House's Red Room. After that, the couples will head to the National Archives for what the White House describes as a viewing of "a variety of important records and documents significant to the American and Chinese relationship throughout history."

From there, Trump will bid Xi farewell, and the whirlwind two-and-a-half day summit, underscored by a palpable tension, will conclude.

The National Archives houses some of America's most important documents, including the U.S. Constitution, the Bill of Rights and the Declaration of Independence.

TRUMP-XI SUMMIT SHOULD MAKE SURE AMERICAN STRENGTH DELIVERS AMERICAN RESULTS

The two heads of state met at the White House on Thursday morning, which began with a state arrival ceremony consisting of military honors, a review of troops, the Chinese and American national anthems and a flyover by a B-2 stealth bomber in formation with four fighter jets. A frenzied press, foreign and domestic, scurried around the White House grounds to catch glimpses of Trump and Xi, who does not often visit the West.

Trump and his administration officials held bilateral talks with the Chinese delegation from the late morning into the early afternoon, lasting for several hours. Xi and Trump also spoke behind closed doors in the Oval Office. After the meetings, Trump escorted Xi to the White House's South Lawn, where the pair viewed Marine One, and the new helipad on which it sits. 

They also toured the White House ballroom, which is under construction, and Trump showed Xi the Presidential Walk of Fame outside the West Wing, which features headshots of presidents past.

Trump installed an image of an autopen in Biden’s place on the Presidential Walk of Fame, a reference to Trump’s repeated attacks on the former president’s use of an autopen while in office. Xi and Trump could both be seen laughing at the image, according to footage on social media.

Outside the White House gates, protesters against Chinese oppression could be heard chanting throughout the day of meetings.

The protests carried into the evening, with chants of "Free Hong Kong," "Xi Jinping, you’re not welcome" and "freedom for political prisoners" at times drowning out the state dinner at the White House, Fox News Digital reported.

XI CAN’T ESCAPE PROTESTERS’ CRIES AT DEAFENING DINNER DEMONSTRATION

A White House official told Fox News Digital before the visit that Trump would explore a wide-ranging deal on possible tariff reductions on non-strategic goods in the meeting with Xi. That official also said the nation's leaders would discuss rare-earth exports and possible export controls, and that Trump was expected to press China to do more to curb fentanyl precursor chemical exports.

Trump called the meeting "great," but didn't elaborate and didn't take questions from the press during the day.

China will send two giant pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, to Zoo Atlanta under a conservation agreement, Xi announced. Xi also invited 100,000 young Americans to visit China for exchanges and study over the next five years.

Xi departed the White House for several hours after the meeting, but returned for a state dinner that officially began at 8:00 p.m. Trump kicked off the dinner with a toast to peace and prosperity for both nations.

Guests at the dinner included the second family, Cabinet officials and their spouses, and titans of industry in banking and tech.

XI PREPARES CHINA ‘FOR BATTLE’ AS EXPERT WARNS OF GRAVE DANGER FACING US AHEAD OF DC SUMMIT

Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, SpaceX founder and former Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) head Elon Musk, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser and Apple Board of Directors Chairman Tim Cook were all in attendance.

The inclusion of American artificial intelligence leaders was notable, given that the powerful technology was a hotbed summit issue as China and the United States race for AI dominance.

item.title: Pope Leo XIV begins historic 4-day visit to France
item.description: Pope Leo XIV's historic France visit includes a private meeting with abuse victims in Lourdes and a Saturday Mass expecting up to 1 million people.
item.content:encoded:
Pope Leo XIV began his visit to France on Friday for his fifth Apostolic Journey as Pontiff. The four-day trip marks the first formal papal visit to the country once called "the eldest daughter of the Church" since Pope Benedict XVI’s visit in September 2008.

French bishops announced the visit’s theme as "That the world may have life," and it comes as the officially secular nation is seeing an influx of new baptisms. So far this year, according to the Conference of Bishops of France, more than 21,000 adults have joined the Church, an increase driven by 18 to 25-year-olds.

"Pope Leo's visit to France has sparked a real tidal wave" of interest, retired French Bishop Marc Stenger told Reuters. "French Catholics are… saying ​loudly that they need the Church to find their way in these uncertain moments in world history."

POPE LEO WARNS AI RISKS BECOMING TOOL OF 'DOMINATION, EXCLUSION AND DEATH' IN NEW ENCYCLICAL

The rise comes after a 2021 report found that some 330,000 French children had been abused by Catholic clergy and lay leaders over seven decades, and said the Church had shown "deep, total and even cruel indifference" ​to victims. Stenger, who led the Diocese of Troyes from 1999 to 2020, told Reuters the scandals "have deeply wounded the Church and damaged its credibility."

In what is described as an unusual move, the Vatican press office announced Pope Leo will meet privately in Lourdes with seven of those victims as part of a message of healing and vulnerability.

SAN FRANCISCO ARCHDIOCESE AGREES TO $395M SETTLEMENT WITH 530 CLERGY ABUSE SURVIVORS

The Vatican calls the trip, "a journey that unites faith and public engagement, memory and the future, with listening and bridge-building at its heart." After being greeted by French President Emmanuel Macron and a courtesy visit to Élysée Palace on Friday, Pope Leo is scheduled to make 15 speeches during his visit. He is expected to speak on several spiritual and societal themes, including the need to protect immigrants, the sick and unborn, and defend human dignity in the era of AI, and address themes of peace, culture, and unity.

French bishops have expressed surprise at the level of interest in the visit. The Associated Press reports organizers for Pope Leo’s Saturday Mass at Paris’ Place de la Concorde, expecting up to 1 million people, have lengthened the security perimeter, extending the site beyond the 1.2-mile length of the Champs-Élysées, where Pope Leo will parade in the Popemobile.

Among his more noteworthy stops, Pope Leo will worship and speak on Sunday at the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes, one of Christianity’s most-visited pilgrimage destinations, especially popular with the sick. It is where an ailing Pope John Paul II, on his final foreign trip in 2004, delivered a forceful condemnation of abortion and euthanasia.

Pope Leo’s visit, however, comes after France’s recent national debate and subsequent passage of legislation allowing adults with incurable illnesses to receive lethal medication. That followed 2024 legislation enshrining abortion as a constitutional right.

POPE LEO PROMOTES ARCHBISHOP WHO BARRED PELOSI FROM COMMUNION TO ONE OF VATICAN'S HIGHEST COURTS

On Friday, Pope Leo will speak at the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, or UNESCO, headquarters in Paris. Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni says Leo will likely reiterate his call for an AI slowdown and speak "with regard to the meaning of existence, to what makes human beings human and what does not."

The speech comes after the Pope’s May manifesto in which Leo warned of the dangers of AI and urged international regulation of the industry. His position again puts him at odds with President Trump, who has encouraged AI innovation so the U.S. can compete with and surpass China.

Following his UNESCO visit, Pope Leo holds a prayer service at the newly-restored Cathedral of Notre-Dame, marking the first papal visit since a 2019 fire nearly destroyed one of France’s national landmarks.

He concludes his trip on Monday with a symbolic full-day visit to the border city of Metz, the birthplace of former French Prime Minister Robert Schuman, considered one of the founding fathers of the European Union. It is a backdrop the Vatican says the Pope will use to "champion friendship among European peoples."

French Ambassador to the Vatican Charles Personnaz told Reuters that Macron has invited leaders from all 27 EU members to attend the speech and meet with the Pontiff. Other media reports say Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy may also attend.

Reuters and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Frontline NATO ally shares shocking take on Russian invasion threat
item.description: Estonia's foreign minister tells Fox News Digital that intelligence sees no Russian buildup for a NATO invasion despite rising hybrid attack fears.
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — Fears that Russia is preparing for a broader war with NATO aren't rattling Estonia's foreign minister, who told Fox News Digital that his country’s intelligence sees no signs Moscow is preparing for a full-scale invasion of the alliance.

"We have more and more this kind of panic in Europe that Russia will invade and will be full-scale aggressive against NATO and Europe and the Baltic states, Poland," Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said in an interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York City before quipping, "But we don’t see it."

Estonia shares a roughly 180-mile border with Russia and has long been among NATO’s most vocal members warning about the threat from Moscow under President Vladimir Putin. But Tsahkna drew a distinction between preparations for a conventional attack and the growing campaign of drone incursions, sabotage, cyberattacks and other provocations that European governments have blamed on Russia.

BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT

"Our intelligence, we see very, very deep into Russia, we don’t see any change," Tsahkna said. "We don’t see that Russia is preparing a full-scale invasion or aggression. The other side of our borders is pretty empty."

Tsahkna, who served as Estonia’s defense minister from 2016 to 2017, contrasted the current picture with what he saw a decade ago, when he said roughly 120,000 Russian troops were positioned across the region’s borders and could be ready to move within 48 hours.

"It’s empty," he said of the Russian side of Estonia’s border today.

His assessment comes as European officials grapple with a series of Russian airspace violations and suspected hybrid attacks, including a Russian military helicopter that crossed into Polish airspace Wednesday. Poland’s military said the incursion appeared to be another attempt to test the readiness of its air defenses.

RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT

European and NATO officials have also warned that Russia could rebuild sufficient military capability to pose a direct threat to the alliance in the coming years. Estonia’s own intelligence service said earlier this year that it saw no Russian intention to attack a NATO member in the immediate term, while warning that Moscow’s military reforms are increasing its longer-term capabilities.

Tsahkna argued that the more immediate threat is a Russian campaign of provocations and hybrid attacks designed to remain below NATO’s Article 5 threshold.

"What Russia is doing now is waging these attacks, which are not crossing Article 5," he said. "It’s sabotage attacks, terror attacks."

"The main purpose for Putin is to play with the Western part of the fear of escalation," Tsahkna went on. "He’s trying to divide the Western parts of the world. Divide the unity, divide this kind of consensus."

Estonia has dealt with GPS interference, cyberattacks and disinformation it has attributed to Russia, while drones have also crossed into its airspace as the war in neighboring Ukraine continues.

Tsahkna said Estonia recorded roughly 40,000 cyberattacks last year, a particular challenge for a country where virtually all public services are available online.

"We are witnessing already, yes, any kind of different level attacks," he said. "Unfortunately, it’s already like normality."

Tsahkna said NATO needs to become more flexible in responding to attacks that fall below the alliance’s collective-defense threshold.

"NATO must be more flex and more dynamic, because these are the attacks which are not crossing Article 5," he said, pointing to sanctions, public attribution and political responses as tools available to the alliance.

"Putin wants to boil Europe and Western part of the world as a frog," Tsahkna said. "Turning on the heat piece by piece is a test of us."

Tsahkna also pointed to an incident last year in which three Russian fighter jets violated Estonian airspace for roughly 12 minutes, prompting Tallinn to request consultations under NATO’s Article 4 and raise the incident at the U.N. Security Council.

He recalled President Donald Trump later saying Russian aircraft that violate NATO airspace should be shot down, and said Estonia has not experienced another comparable fighter-jet incursion since.

"We have now drones coming in," Tsahkna said. "NATO is working as a Swiss clock."

Tsahkna said NATO may need cheaper and more efficient ways to bring down drones rather than relying on expensive fighter aircraft.

On Ukraine, Tsahkna called for increasing pressure on Moscow, arguing that Russia’s economic and battlefield losses could eventually push Putin toward serious negotiations.

"What we see, and I also visited Ukraine last week, is that we need to put more pressure on Russia, because Putin understands only very clear language through strength," he said.

Tsahkna also pointed to Ukraine’s growing ability to strike targets deep inside Russia as a source of pressure on the Kremlin.

"If Putin is under heavier pressure, and also Ukraine is delivering more deep-strike capabilities and attacks, there will be a momentum when Putin may really start some kind of ceasefire or energy ceasefire, or real talks," he said.

Tsahkna said Trump had devoted significant effort to seeking an end to the war, but argued that Putin has used the diplomatic process to buy time.

"President Trump has put lots of energy during the last year to find a way, but Putin has just played with him and also winning the time," Tsahkna said.

He said Ukraine’s deep strikes are already weakening Russia economically, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly signaled his willingness to agree to a ceasefire.

"Putin can just decide like today or tomorrow to have a ceasefire," Tsahkna said. "Unfortunately, we don’t see any change for now."

Tsahkna also said Estonia has been assured that U.S. forces will remain in the region for the next rotation, amid the Trump administration’s broader review of the American military footprint in Europe.

"We got the information that it will happen soon," he said of the next rotation.

Tsahkna said the presence of American forces remains an important part of deterrence on NATO’s eastern flank.

"U.S. troops are keeping the peace in our region," Tsahkna said. "The flag of the troops is so important to give the message to President Putin" about the red lines between Russia and NATO.

item.title: GOP handed new lifeline on biggest pocketbook fight of midterms
item.description: Club for Growth's memo urges Republicans to blame federal expansion for high cost of living and resist subsidies ahead of the November midterms.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: Republicans are being given a new playbook on an issue that is all but certain to be the biggest political lightning rod of the November midterms.

Conservative group Club for Growth is sending a memo to Capitol Hill lawmakers on Friday arguing that Americans' struggle with high living costs cannot be ignored — and that the fault lies with an expanding federal government.

"Americans are not asking whether the inflation rate has slowed; they are asking why the same basket of goods is permanently more expensive," the information packets being distributed to Republican lawmakers read. It's an argument that could be a lifeline for the GOP as it fights an uphill battle to keep control of the House and Senate. The materials, a two-page memo for lawmakers and a more in-depth 76-page policy packet, also urge Republicans to push policies that Club for Growth says will actually lower those costs.

AMERICA’S BROKEN PERMITTING SYSTEM IS QUIETLY RAISING YOUR COST OF LIVING

The strategy would be a gamble, given the midterms are traditionally a referendum on how people feel about how they are doing under the party currently in power. But it gives Republicans a potential economic platform and a roadmap to pitch for lowering costs if they keep the majority for the next two years.

"The free-market answer is structural cost relief: spend less, build more, produce more energy, make healthcare compete, let workers earn, and let families choose," the memo said.

BILLIONS SPENT BY KEY FEDERAL AGENCY HASN'T MADE AMERICAN DREAM OF HOMEOWNERSHIP ANY EASIER: REPORT

It urged Republicans to resist calling for subsidies for areas of the economy where prices are skyrocketing, arguing that handing out taxpayer money would only increase costs in the longer-term. An example the memo used is Affordable Care Act (ACA) premium tax credits, which Republicans have long blamed for skyrocketing healthcare costs before the COVID-era subsidy expired at the beginning of this year.

"Subsidies and regulation function as a back door for government control and involvement in private industry," the memo argued. "The only way to address the affordability crisis properly is to undo misguided government intervention and stop pretending more of the same will suddenly work."

But it could put GOP lawmakers at odds with President Donald Trump and his promise to give each American adult $5,000 if Republicans win the midterms. Several GOP lawmakers who spoke with Fox News Digital last week were hesitant to embrace the idea.

Among the solutions offered are reforming Social Security, which fiscal hawks have long warned will soon run out of cash if changes are not made to current age requirements and other guidelines.

GOP FISCAL HAWK SOUNDS ALARM ON 'OUT OF CONTROL' FEDERAL SPENDING, SAYING 'BOTH PARTIES HAVE FAILED US'

On high housing costs, the memo urges lawmakers to increase supply by targeting land use and building regulations rather than offering subsidies to make existing housing more affordable.

Energy costs, which were a flashpoint in the 2025 off-year elections as well, could be brought down by furthering the Trump administration's goals to unleash U.S. energy sources rather than Democrats' push for net-zero carbon emissions, the memo said.

A focus on nuclear energy policies could also help drive down energy costs, which will be at the forefront of most Americans' minds during the November election.

And while Democrats have pushed free early childcare as a solution for struggling families, the Club for Growth memo is urging Republicans to find a more lasting solution in reforming regulations surrounding the industry.

"Health and safety training in specific areas, adherence to building, fire, and health codes, and comprehensive background checks, including fingerprinting, are reasonable," the memo said. "However, strict and complex rules about work-child ratios, rigid staffing mandates, and regulations on facility specifications, including equipment requirements and zoning classifications, increase operating costs without demonstrable improvements in child wellbeing."

The election is less than 50 days away, and both sides are working overtime to prove they are best positioned to help ease rising costs.

item.title: Fast-food drive-thrus took over American mornings for these key reasons
item.description: Fast-food breakfast and the drive-thru have become daily rituals for millions of Americans. A food historian reveals how this once-novel concept became an everyday staple.
item.content:encoded:
For millions of Americans, grabbing breakfast or coffee from a fast-food drive-thru is an ordinary part of the morning routine — but not long ago, ordering a meal without leaving the car was a novelty.

So how did the drive-thru go from a novel idea to an everyday staple?

Convenience and an "on-the-go" lifestyle are two big factors, according to Capri Cafaro, the creator, executive producer and host of "America the Bountiful."

MORE AMERICANS NOW EAT IN THEIR CARS THAN EVER BEFORE AS EXPERT REVEALS WHAT IT SAYS ABOUT MODERN LIFE

Cafaro spoke with Fox News Digital about how and why the drive-thru, particularly drive-thru breakfast, became a daily ritual for many Americans.

There is some debate over which restaurant pioneered the drive-thru concept.

West Coast chain In-N-Out Burger is widely credited with creating the first drive-thru, debuting a two-way intercom drive-thru system in California in 1948.

AMERICA'S LATE-NIGHT FAST-FOOD CULTURE MAY BE MAKING A COMEBACK — HERE'S WHY

However, Cafaro and other news publications, maintain that Springfield, Mo., restaurant Red's Giant Hamburg (the word "hamburger" reportedly didn't fit on the sign) actually introduced the drive-thru concept in 1947, narrowly beating In-N-Out.

Regardless of which establishment first created it, the drive-thru emerged at a time when Americans' relationship with the automobile was rapidly changing.

During the mid-20th century, the country saw a surge in automobile usage due to the growth of suburbs and the rise of highways, particularly the interstate system and Route 66, which will celebrate its 100th anniversary in November.

More people took to the roads, not just for their daily commute to and from work, but also for road trips and family outings.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

As Americans ended up behind the wheel, "that really created an opportunity for the rise of fast-food restaurants and certainly the drive-thru," Cafaro noted.

Despite McDonald's firm grip on the fast-food breakfast market in recent years, it was not the first chain to introduce the morning meal.

McDonald's was actually beaten to the punch by Jack in the Box, which debuted breakfast in 1969 with the Breakfast Jack, a sandwich with egg, cheese and ham.

The Egg McMuffin, by comparison, wasn't on McDonald's menus until 1971, when it was invented at a Santa Barbara, Calif., location by franchise owner Herb Peterson, according to the McDonald's website.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"McDonald's. It seems to be the most prolific and the most recognizable, [but] they actually … were later adopters to some of these trends that are so embedded in our fast-food culture today," Cafaro said.

The golden arches didn't hover over a drive-thru window until 1975, when McDonald's added one to its Sierra Vista, Arizona, location to accommodate soldiers who weren't allowed to get out of their cars while wearing their uniforms off-base, its website said.

Today, drive-thru sales account for roughly 70% of McDonald's business, according to the corporate website.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Another late adopter of the drive-thru is Starbucks. The coffee giant didn't open its first drive-thru location until 1994.

Business Insider reported in 2022 that two-thirds of Starbucks sales happen via the drive-thru.

"The drive-thru and fast-food landscape has changed in the last 50 to 70 years, and it will continue to evolve as long as we have cars and as long as we want convenience," Cafaro said.

But there is a remarkably simple way to stop them.

Clearly define who is eligible to play in the Women’s National Basketball Association.

THE WOMEN'S NATIONAL BASKETBALL ASSOCIATION CAN'T DEFINE A 'WOMAN,' AND IT'S BEYOND SHAMEFUL

Funny how quickly a hypothetical becomes real when somebody finally has to write the rule.

Last week, I wrote that the WNBA had backed itself into a corner.

Turns out somebody at league headquarters finally noticed the walls.

WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert has now told teams that the league is discussing transgender-player eligibility and expects those conversations to continue.

Good.

It's about time.

Because the WNBA doesn't need another statement.

It needs a definition.

The league's collective bargaining agreement says:

"Only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA."

Seems pretty straightforward.

Except it doesn't define what a woman is.

That might have been an amusing legal omission when the question was theoretical.

It isn't anymore.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Former NBA players Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White say they want to enter the WNBA Draft.

They're making a point.

French transgender basketball player Julie Tétart, who is biologically male, is already playing professional women's basketball overseas.

Suddenly the question isn't something being shouted across cable-news panels.

It's an eligibility question.

For a professional sports league.

The WNBA has a courage problem and it’s not Sophie Cunningham

And the answer can't be: We'll get back to you.

So what’s the standard?

Biological sex?

Gender identity?

Hormone levels?

Medical transition?

Pick one.

Write it down.

Apply it equally.

Because you can't have a professional women's league whose rule says only women may play

while refusing to define who qualifies.

That's not a rule.

That's a future lawsuit with a basketball.

And while league officials figure this out, we're getting a pretty good demonstration of why this

subject has become so difficult for the WNBA to address honestly.

Just look at what's happening in Indiana.

DiJonai Carrington came up behind Sophie Cunningham on a fast break and clobbered her in the

head, sending her crashing to the floor and bloodying her mouth.

Carrington was assessed a Flagrant 2 and ejected.

Right call.

It wasn’t even close to a basketball move.

Afterward, Fever coach Stephanie White defended Carrington's competitiveness and said she

didn't believe Carrington was trying to hurt Cunningham.

As White spoke, Makayla Timpson looked down.

Caitlin Clark buried her head in her hands.

Interesting reaction.

White has since said she hadn't seen the foul when she made those comments.

There's a problem.

Video appears to show White looking directly toward the play as it happens.

Locked in.

The WNBA has a courage problem and it’s not Sophie Cunningham

Now, looking isn't necessarily seeing.

Maybe she missed the contact.

Watch the video.

Decide for yourself.

Then came another press conference.

This time White talked about unity, love, grace and integrity while blasting the outside forces she

says are trying to divide the Fever and "hijack" the WNBA.

Right before she said, "Everybody else can go to hell."

Hmm.

But she’s right about one thing.

Too many people are trying to turn every WNBA game into something other than basketball.

But here's the problem.

Most of those forces aren't coming from outside.

The WNBA invited them in.

For years the league has embraced political and cultural causes far beyond basketball.

Players have been celebrated for speaking out.

Coaches have spoken out.

The league has spoken out.

Broadcasters have spoken out.

Fine.

Not really.

Somewhere in there is a basketball game.

But you don't get to invite politics and cultural activism onto the court when you agree with the

message and then complain that outsiders are hijacking basketball when the questions become

uncomfortable.

That's not how this works.

Which is why I've been impressed with Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham.

They've backed their coach.

They should.

That's what professionals do.

The WNBA has a courage problem and it’s not Sophie Cunningham

Cunningham doesn't need to attack her coach every time someone sticks a microphone in her

face to prove what she believes.

Her position is clear.

She believes boys shouldn't compete in girls' sports.

She said it.

She stood by it.

And she’s standing by her coach and teammates.

That’s courage.

And courage isn't screaming the loudest.

Sometimes it's standing your ground without burning down the locker room around you.

Clark doesn't need another national controversy attached to her name either.

These women have something else to do.

Play basketball.

They have teammates depending on them.

Games to win.

A championship to chase.

Maybe the adults running the league could help them out.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Start by answering the question.

And while we're at it, perhaps the people covering the WNBA could ask it.

Not another question about inclusion.

Not another question about the political climate.

Not another invitation for a prepared statement.

Ask the basketball question.

What objective standard determines who is eligible to play in the Women's National Basketball

Association?

Ask Cathy Engelbert.

Then follow up.

Would Enes Kanter Freedom qualify?

Would Royce White?

Would Julie Tétart?

The WNBA has a courage problem and it’s not Sophie Cunningham

If the answers are different, why?

This is what sports journalists are supposed to do.

Ask questions.

Especially uncomfortable ones.

The tragedy is that the WNBA is sitting on an extraordinary opportunity.

Caitlin Clark brought millions of new eyeballs to women's basketball.

Audiences grew.

New fans arrived.

The league finally had what every professional sports organization spends decades trying to build: Momentum.

And somehow the conversation keeps becoming about everything except the basketball.

Race.

Politics.

Gender.

Protests.

Officiating controversies.

Culture wars.

Eventually fans get tired.

They didn't buy a ticket to attend a sociology seminar.

They came to watch basketball.

And that's why Engelbert's eligibility discussions matter.

The league has an opportunity to remove at least one enormous source of ambiguity.

Define the women's category.

Clearly.

Fairly.

Objectively.

Then enforce it.

This debate does not have to be about inclusion.

Transgender people should be treated with dignity and respect.

The WNBA has a courage problem and it’s not Sophie Cunningham

It’s about protection and fair competition.

Women deserve their own athletic category.

And yes, there are people who vehemently disagree with that.

Activists do.

Some members of the media do.

Some WNBA players and coaches do.

Fine.

Then have the courage to have the debate.

But first, the league has to have the courage to define its own rules.

The WNBA keeps saying outside forces are trying to hijack women's basketball.

Fine.

Then take the issue away from them.

Write the rule.

Define eligibility.

Tell the players.

Tell the coaches.

Tell the broadcasters.

Tell the fans.

Tell Enes Kanter Freedom.

Tell Royce White.

Tell Julie Tétart.

Tell everybody exactly what the W stands for.

And then do something increasingly novel for the Women's National Basketball Association.

Go play basketball.

item.title: The worst bet in America isn't Kalshi or Polymarket. It's hiding in plain sight
item.description: Americans spent over $113 billion on lottery tickets in 2024, yet Powerball and Mega Millions offer some of the worst odds in all of gambling.
item.content:encoded:
America suddenly has a gambling problem.

Sports betting is everywhere. Prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket let people wager on everything from football games to elections. Politicians and regulators are asking whether we've gone too far.

Fair question.

SEN DAVE MCCORMICK: PREDICTION MARKETS ARE BOOMING. WASHINGTON MUST CATCH UP

But there's another gambling operation that's been sitting on street corners for decades, quietly pickpocketing people. The government lottery. And it may offer some of the worst bets in America.

Americans bought more than $113 billion in lottery products in fiscal 2024, according to the North American Association of State and Provincial Lotteries. That's more than $300 million every single day.

GREED MEETS GREED: DRAFTKINGS TO CLOSE ITS WRIGLEY FIELD SPORTSBOOK AT THE END OF MAY OVER ILLINOIS TAX

And business is booming. Census Bureau data show state lottery ticket sales nearly doubled from $52.8 billion in 2008 to $104.7 billion in 2024. Apparently inflation hasn't killed America's appetite for becoming an instant millionaire.

Let's start with Powerball. Your odds of winning the jackpot are approximately 1 in 292.2 million. Mega Millions? 1 in 290.5 million.

You could buy one Mega Millions ticket every week for 100 years and purchase only about 5,200 tickets. Those aren't just bad odds.

LUCKY TRAVELER WINS $3.3M JACKPOT ON 'WHEEL OF FORTUNE' SLOT MACHINE AT HARRY REID INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT

They're astronomical odds.

Yet lotteries have gotten increasingly creative at selling the dream. Mega Millions increased its ticket price from $2 to $5, promising bigger starting jackpots and built-in prize multipliers. Now Powerball is getting into football with a $5 NFL-themed game across nearly two dozen states.

FANATICS SPORTSBOOK LAUNCHES PROGRAM TO IDENTIFY, PUNISH SPORTS BETTORS WHO THREATEN ATHLETES ON SOCIAL MEDIA

Then there are scratch-offs. Walk into almost any convenience store, and you'll see an entire wall of them. $5. $10. $20. Even $50 scratch-off tickets.

We're not selling a little $1 fantasy anymore. We're selling some expensive dreams.

BRYCE HARPER VIDEO TO FANDUEL USER WITH GAMBLING ADDICTION UNDER REVIEW BY PENNSYLVANIA OFFICIALS

Here's where the lottery bothers me most. A wealthy person spending $20 on lottery tickets generally doesn't matter financially. But someone living paycheck to paycheck or making $50,000 a year spending $20 every week is blowing more than $1,000 a year.

For a lower-income household, that's real money. That's an emergency fund. That's credit-card debt. That's a Roth IRA contribution.

Invest $1,000 annually for 30 years earning a hypothetical 8%, and you could accumulate more than $113,000. Instead, that money may be disappearing one scratch-off at a time.

STEVE MOORE, ED POZZUOLI: STOP FUNDING SCHOOL SYSTEMS. LET THE MONEY FOLLOW THE CHILD

That's why economists have long raised concerns about lotteries being effectively regressive. The issue isn't necessarily who spends the most dollars. It's how large that spending is as a percentage of someone's income.

Here's my favorite part. When somebody trades on Kalshi or Polymarket, suddenly we're worried they're gambling. When somebody repeatedly hands money to a state lottery? We're funding education! That's some pretty good marketing.

To be fair, lotteries do fund legitimate government programs. U.S. lotteries transferred nearly $30.6 billion to government beneficiaries in fiscal 2024, supporting education, veterans, senior programs and other public purposes.

Great. But let's call the transaction what it is. Government is raising revenue by selling its citizens extremely long odds of becoming rich. And unlike prediction markets, there's no research that's going to help you pick six random numbers.

No earnings report. No polling data. No economic forecast. Just luck.

Prediction markets deserve scrutiny. Sports betting deserves scrutiny. And people absolutely need to understand the risks of gambling. But government lotteries shouldn't get some moral exemption simply because the proceeds fund popular programs.

Buy a Powerball ticket for entertainment. Grab a scratch-off for your birthday. Dream about the mansion and Ferrari. Just don't confuse any of it with building wealth.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Because in almost every form of gambling, there's an old saying we’ve heard for decades: The house always wins.

With America's lottery system, there's just one interesting twist. The house is your government.
